newsitem.title: GERMANY: European photo industry focuses on hi-tech.
newsitem.headline: European photo industry focuses on hi-tech.

text.p: Europe's photographic industry is banking on a big boost from increased availiability of Advanced Photo System technology and new digital cameras, both on show at the sector's biggest trade fair this week.

Industry analysts said on Tuesday that APS, which offers easier film loading and a choice of three different picture formats, got off to a slow start after its launch in April this year but retailers were now optimistic about its prospects.
Several firms will present new APS models at Photokina, the bi-annual World Fair for Imaging, which opens in Cologne on Wednesday and runs until next Monday.
"We're seeing the launch of more and more APS cameras highlighting the full range of APS features," Marion Knoche, a director of German market research firm GfK said.
The simple pleasures of taking snaps have become big business. GfK research indicates 570 million films and 40 million cameras were sold in Europe last year.

Knoche said a recent survey of European retailers found they believed APS films and cameras could achieve 20 percent market share by the end of the year, giving sales figures for the sector in Europe a welcome pickup after a sluggish first half.
"There's no doubt that APS got off to a serious false start," said Rainer Schmidt, managing director of Germany's Photoindustrie-Verband industry association.
"The scientists had done their work but there were initial problems with marketing and delivery," Schmidt said. "We're hoping for a bigger breakthrough now."

APS film, developed jointly by the so-called Big Five -- Eastman Kodak, Canon USA Inc, Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd, Minolta Corp and Nikon Inc -- is smaller than existing 35mm film and includes a magnetic strip which records data about each frame.
This information -- such as in what conditions the picture was taken -- helps laboratories to make a better job of developing the pictures.
"What we hope for most from Photokina is that the public will gain a better understanding and awareness of the technologies which the sector is offering," Schmidt said.

That technology includes digital cameras, which do not use film but instead save the images they see on hard disk. They are then processed on computer, allowing the user to play around and alter the size and shape of the image.

"At the Photokina this year we're seeing the first digital cameras under 1,000 marks ($660)," said Knoche. "Our research inducates we'll see some growth in the digital market next year and it'll certainly be a force to be reckoned with in 1998."
